Cuap. XI.

Poor innocent infant should be suffered to famish for another’s sin? Yet if the latter be left together with the legitimate issue, they shall not easily challenge to be admitted to equal shares, unless the parents made express declaration to this purpose.

In reference to the several parts of maintenance, upon the parents decease during the minority of the children, the inheritance is not only theirs if he died intestate, but farther, it cannot rightly be taken from them by his express will, so far as is necessary for obtaining this end. For it doth not seem probable that a child of these years should be capable of committing any such offence as might render him unworthy of so needful a support.

IV. VII. Whatever exceeds this proportion of maintenance, is due to the children, when able to provide for themselves, not so much by any express command of the law of nature, as upon this principle, that commonly speaking, parents desire that none should fare better than their own children. Therefore, it was a very singular disposition, that of Crates the Theban, who lodged his money in the hands of a banker upon these terms: that if his children proved ignorant, it should be vested to them; but if they happened to be philosophers, it should be distributed among the common people; because men of that profession could be in want of nothing. As to what some have advanced, that parents get all for the sake of their children, and therefore the children, even in the parents lifetime, have such a right to their goods as shall be valued against them in other cases, beyond the necessaries of maintenance; this is absolutely false: For, every man in his getting hath first of all an eye to himself, and labours chiefly on his own account. Horat. lib. ii. Epift. 2.v. 190, ec.

But what remains above his private necessaries, he is willing should pass to those who are dearest to him, as commonly, his children are presumed to be. And children have thus far only a peculiar title to hope for their parents estate, as that in case of no express will to the contrary, their claim is preferred to all others; and because it very rarely happens, that parents are induced to lay aside their children in intestacy.

It is well enacted by the Roman laws, that every parent who disinheirits his child shall be obliged expressly to give his reason for so doing; and that some certain causes only shall be sufficient to justify him in this proceeding. Nay farther, the same laws gave the disinherited children an action de inoffuivfs toftamento; of a hle wet mesic nverdivg to natural affection and duty. The delicacy of which was not to bring into dispute whether or no the testator had a power of transmitting his goods to others rather than to his children, upon just causes; but to discuss and examine the reasons which moved the deceased to make a settlement contrary to the common inclinations of mankind. And if, upon such a hearing, it was discovered that the father thus neglected his issue, either through his own absurd fancy and humour, or through the fraudulent intrusion of others, the inheritance was by public authority avowed to those to whom it would otherwise have descended, had the father consulted with reason and conscience in his last disposition. And therefore Cicero well replies upon Evucius, who charged his client Rifeizs with a design to disinherit his own son: je cughe to have been the basaasfs of the clowler, to live capite at the sins and vices of the young, which might be supposed able to incense the father to such a betgie as that he should once entertain a kofdatiini ding violence to nature itself, of banishing that affection which was so deeply rected in his musi; and, in a word, of forgetting utterly that he was a father.

It is remarkable under what colour the disinherited children, by the same laws, moved so relict: for it being necessary that they should ground their complaint on a supposition that the cause of their disinheritance was unjust, they pretended in the form of the action, that their parents at the time of making such a will were not using their reason.

Still, as to other matters, a father ought so to favour his children as not to lay aside his just regard to other duties. Hence, when he may be judged to have made sufficient provision for his own family, he is not in the least hindered from employing his goods in acts of gratitude and liberality, though to the lessening of his children's fortunes. Thus in case a man hath either received extraordinary kindnesses from another, criavle by a seasonable beneficence to put some great genius, now struggling with poverty, into a way of doing great service; what reason is there but that he should be allowed to devise some part of his goods to such excellent uses? It’s plain, antiquity highly celebrated the action of King Azalus, who had this ordinary affection. Having been obliged by his former examens with very

VIII. Neither doth a Father lie under any Necessity of dividing his Goods among his Children in equal Shares; but he may assign to one or two somewhat above the rest, as an extraordinary Bounty; either on account of singular Merit, or of great and illustrious Hopes, or even of particular Affection *.
So likewise in distributing Portions, a just regard may be had to the Credit of the Family, that it may hereafter retain its Strength and Splendor. If this Interest cannot be secured upon an equal Division of the Patrimony between many Children, the Father may, without any breach of the Law of Nature, devise the chief part of his Goods to one, and command the rest to fit down contented with smaller Portions. Hence the Rights of Primogeniture * obtain’d among many Nations, which according to the most ancient Institution, conferred on the eldest Son the regal Government of the Family, the domestic Priesthood *, and double Share of what his Father possessed, Which double Proportion was designed to defray the charge of Entertainments, and of religious Ceremonies; as Grotius receives >*.

On the contrary there have not been wanting Nations, where the younger Brothers succeed to the largest Share of the Inheritance, or at least have their Option, to choose what part they like.

Which Custom is built on this Principle, That the elder Brethren have for a long time enjoyed the Benefit of Education from their Parents; of which the younger being often deprived by too untimely a Loss, they deserve some Consideration to requite and comfort them under their Disadvantage.

Though the latter of these Institutions seems more agreeable to low and mean Families, the former to the great and noble.

The Laws have better contrived it than we can, and we had better commit a Mistake by their Direction, than hazard it rashly
by our own Choice. They are not properly ours, since a civil Prescription made without us has designed for the good of our
Succeffors. And though we have some liberty allowed by them, yet I take it to be the greatest and most apparent Cause, why
many are deprived of those Estates to which their good Fortune entitled them, and common Justice would have given them,

Chapter XI.

Every Right termed, The Right of Representation; by virtue of which Children are supposed to take the place of their deceased Parents, so as to be allowed the same in the partition of the patrimonial inheritance as their Father, were he now living, would receive and consequently to succeed on the level with those who stand in the Father's degree. And it would indeed be a lamentable misfortune, if, besides the untimely loss of their Father, they should farther be deprived of those 2s which either the rule of the law, or the distribution of their Progenitors had given their Parents just hopes of enjoying. But if in any place the equal constitutions will not admit of this representative right, the Children, who have been so unhappily bereaved of their Father and of their Hopes, must endeavour to bear the calamity as an affliction which Providence hath laid upon them.

Upon failure of such in the first, and the other delving degrees, Respon suggested that Liberatam ought to take back into the line of ascents, as well in consideration that, for the most part, either the possessives themselves, or at least the first seeds and principles of them, which the Children afterwards increased, proceed from the Parents; 28 because their extraordinary benefits give them an especial title to this reward: Who, since they would much rather have desired that their Children should inherit their fortunes, yet when they survived them, contrary to the ordinary course of nature, "twas but equitable they should receive, however, this melancholy comfort, of succeeding to what the Children possessed. This a condition (as Ficoleves) ab daitly unhappy, for a Father to be the sole heir of his own sowing? Panegyr. c. 38. Vid. Iv. t.2. 1. 15. D. De inoffic. testam. Lib, xxix. t. 4. D. Philo the Jew *, reporting, "That AT hath established this order of inheritance, 'the Sons should [and
the Daughters next, then the Brothers, and in the fourth place the Uncles by the Father's side, which
vies as an argument to prove, that Fathers likewise may inherit what their Sons leave behind; For *twould
be first (fays he) to imagine, that the Uncle should be acknowledged to succeed his Brother's son, as a near kin
may to the Father, and yet the Father himself be abridged of that privilege. But inasmuch as the law of nature
appoints, that Children shall be heirs to their Parents, and not Parents to their Children, Motus passed this case over in silence, as ominous and unlucky, and contrary to all pious fives and delves - Let the Father and Mother soon to be Cainers by the immature death of their Children, who ought to be affiled with more explicable grief, vs dying the right of inheritance to the Uncles, he obliquely admits the claim of the Parents, both for the preservation of decency and order, and for continuing the line in the same family.

Some Parents too have the additional title of an infirm and indigent old age; under which sad condition their Children were otherwise obliged to maintain them: As one of the Artic Laws explicity enjoined 2. Tertius Orat. Vi. The Law commands by to maintain our Parents, under which now are comprehended not only our Father and Mother, but our Grandfather, for theses are the fittest of our kindred, and from these descend the Goods and Fortunes which their Posterity enjoy. Thefe therefore we are necessarily bound to support, even the t. cy should have thing to leave us. Add. Grot. d.l. Se&t.5. & Ziegler ad d.l.
Yet in cases Father hath without reason grievously hated and injured his Son, without any subsequent reconciliation, the Son may justly exclude him from the right of inheritance3. The same with him who exposed his Son, when an infant, utterly neglecting his support: For here no doubt the claim of the foster-father, who hath undertaken the care and burden of the child's education, ought first to be admitted. Nay, farther it seems reasonable, that an adoptive Father should in this point be preferred to a natural Parent; that he may recover what he hath expended on bringing up another’s Child. We are likewise to observe, that the Lawyers do not admit of representation in the ascending line, as they do in the descending 3 that is, if a Man die without Law, leaving a Daughter, and a Grand-father by his Mother's side, the latter of these shall not be allowed to make claim in the room of his Daughter. A rule which seems to be grounded on this consideration, that naturally the hopes of succession do not ascend, but descend: Wherefore, the Son had indeed hopes of succeeding his Father, and might transmit the same hopes to his own issue; but the Mother had never any hope or desire of inheriting after her Children; and so could not, contrary to the order of nature, convey back any such hope to her own Parents: And consequently, the nearer claimant here excludes very justly the more remote +.

IV. Were the descending and the ascending Lines both tail, the Succession to intestates devolves on the collateral Kindred. As to the order in which they are to be admitted, where the civil Statutes do not expressly settle it, 'tis to be determined by what natural Conjecture : Which always favours that Person whom we presume to have fled most in the Affection of the deceavd ; yet so as that we measure this Affection more by the common Inclination of wise and sober Men, and according as it tends to the Prevention of Quarrels, can by the moral Humour of some few particular Persons.
Now, according to the Judgment of wise Men, natural Reason in this Case pays an especial Regard to Warrant of Blood, yet so as at the same time to consider from what Source the respective Possessions seemed to flow to the deceas'd *, or who formerly parted with any thing, or suffered any Loss upon account of his coming into the World.
'Though Livor's first Rate + is, The Affection between Parents and Children; and his next, The Love between Brethren, arising from their Relation to the same common Stock, and improved by the likenesses of Years and Education. After these follow Brothers' Children, and other Relations joined to us by virtue of that frarinal Union. And then (all thefe being first considered, whom Nature, as it were, necessitates us to love and esteem) in the last Place those are admitted, whom either past Kindness or Agreeableness of Temper and Manners, or peculiar Likeness of Inclinations, or known Fidelity, recommends and encourages. Zussi § places the Degrees of Kindred in the Order following: The first Society is in E D C Dlock ; the men in Children 5 it comes then to a Family, and a Community of all things. The Relation of Brethren comes next ; and after that, of Brothers and Sisters' Children ; who, when they are too many for one House, are transplanted into others, as into Colonies, And then follow Matches and Alliances, with increase of Kindness, consequent upon them. Now the Relation of Blood and the Kindness that arises from it vouchsafes even to Men one another.

XV. But the high Encomiums given to Friendship in Authors may raise a Doubt, whether Friends are not sometimes to be preferred to Relations? Of all Sweets, Lays Tullius, none hath more of Excellency, or of Strength, than when good Men, alike in Manners, are united by a familiar Acquaintance,

And indeed it frequently happens, that we take
more Satisfaction in the Company and Conversation
of an indifferent Person, than of one related to
in Blood, and intrust many things with the Score
and Fidelity of the former, which we conceal from
the latter. In fine, we address ourselves more
duly to serve the Friend than the Relation; because
he, on the other side, is the more ready of the two
to assist us in any Difficulty.

But it cannot hence be concluded, That by virtue of a general Custom, coming up almost to Force of a Law, a Friend is to take place of Relations, though the deceased Party should chance to have expressed more Tokens of Affection towards him, than towards them. For in the Business of transmitting an Inheritance, we are not guided only by Kindness and Good-will, but consider farther, on whom 'tis most proper and convenient that our Fortunes should descend. Since Men are carried on by a general Propensity to with the Family in as good a Condition as possible from which they derive their Original, therefore *tis commonly most convenient that our Goods should continue in our own Line. Besides, 'tis a necessary Consequence to say, I was highly delighted with this Person's Familiarity and Conversation, therefore *twas my Inclination likewise to transmit my Possessions upon him. For this Friendship between Persons not allied in Race, generally extends no farther, than to a mutual Signification of Good will, a Communication of Designs, and the ordinary Services and Offices of Life. But before I can be conceived to have joined Houses, as it were, with a Stranger, by conveying to him my Estate, 'twill be necessary to produce an express and legal Will to this Purpose. Thus, although according to ancient Manners of the Romans, in the Order of common Duties, After Parents and Children, the first Place was given to Pupils or Wards ; the second to Clients or Dependents * ; the third to Guests ; the last to the Kindred by Blood and Marriage, ac

Cuap. XI.

Inheritance was beyond all Controversy due. We cannot be denied, but that under this ample Power of disposing of Goods by Testament, there crept in, as well at Athens as at Rome, a prodigious Spawn of Cheats, like a peftilential Infection; such as parasitical Flattery and Inveigling, especially of old and childish Persons, Circumventions, Forgery of Writings, and the like.

Bodinus* chiefly objects against these testamentary Constitutions of Solon, that they allowed Men to bequeath by Will Real as well as Personal Estates. By which means, as he observes, whilst many of those Estates might happen to fall on one Person, there arose a vast Inequality of Wealth between the Subjects, whence the Poor grew envious towards the Rich; the Rich proud and insolent towards the Poor; Mischiefs that have a peculiar Tendency to the disturbing and subverting of Government: Especially since the Proverb is often made good, That the more a Man hath, the more he shall have. But Bodinus observes, that 'tis the interest of States, where the supreme Power is lodged in the People, to take care that some few Persons do not exceed the rest by too vast a Disproportion. Which likewise was the Reason of that Few Law, forbidding the perpetual Alienation of Land; and of that other, by which Women who had received Land in Inheritance were enjoined to marry into their own Tribe, lest otherwise the Land should pass from one Tribe to another °.

Aristotle, among his Rules for preserving a democratical Government, gives this as one, that Inheritances should descend not by Testament, but by Kindred, and that no Person shall have more than one Inheritance, because thus the Fortunes of Men will be kept more upon a Level. What Mischiefs were introduced into the Spartan Commonwealth by that Liberty of Testaments, which Ephorus set up in opposition to Lycurgus’s Laws, may be read at large in Plutarch’s Life of Agis*. Among other Nations, Men were allowed no Liberty in this Point; or if they had any such Privilege, it was very much abridged and restrained.

Of the Hebrew Laws in this Particular, Selden* and Grotius* give a full Account. Of the ancient Germans, Tacitus reports, that they had no such things as Wills or Testaments, but every Man's Children were his Heirs and Successors; and, in default of Children, those of the next Degree, as Brothers and Uncles by both Parents. Which Place of the Historian, why we should interpret with some in this manner, that the Germans, who had not yet learnt the use of Letters, did not make use of formal and written Wills after the Roman Custom, which Tacitus for the most part hath an Eye to in that Description, we cannot yet find sufficient Reason. For among the Romans themselves Wills by Word of Mouth * and without Writing were also allowed. And therefore if Tacitus had designed to observe, that only written Wills were those with which the Germans were acquainted; he would have expressed himself more particularly and distinctly.

Besides, what the Rights of Kin were honoured with the highest Reverence and most sacred Veneration among those People, appears from what the same Historian afterwards remarks. The greater number of Relations any Man hath, whether by Blood or by Marriage, the more Respect is paid him in his Old Age: Nor are any Rewards allowed to compute Persons under the Misfortune of being childless. Every one books on it as his necessary Obligation, to undertake the Quarrels of his Father or of any near Kinsman, as well as their Friendships and Alliances. In many parts of Germany at this Day, if a Man hath a Son born to him, 'tis an usual Expression to say, He hath got an Heir.

Again, it doth not appear why a Nation, such as the old Germans then were, quite ignorant of the ways of heaping up Wealth, content with the poor accommodation of household Conveniences, and scarcely desiring any farther Aggrandizement from their Fields, their Cattle, and their Pains in burning, than a daily Subsistence; why such a Nation should have any Reason to desire the privilege of Testaments. It being an idle and unnecessary Care, for those who follow this way of Life, to covet to themselves any large Extent of Land. Nor is the making of a Will so necessary a consequence of Property, but that a State or People may introduce some one uniform Method of Inheritance, without any such express Disposition. And this will especially hold good of that People, who, as Tacitus informs us, assigned such a Tract of Land to such a number of People; why afterwards parcelled it out into private shares, according to the Worth and Esteem of particular Princes. It is said, that these Men were wont, however, at their Death, to leave some sort of Orders and Injunctions to their Family, we deny that every Act of this kind comes up to the nature of a Testament*.

This method of Succession, as 'tis the most plain and simple, and most agreeable to the common Inclinations of Nature, so hath it an especial Tendency to the keeping up an equal Proportion in the Wealth of the Subjects, to the securing a Supply of Natives in a just and proper Number, and to the preserving the Estates and the perpetuity of Families'.

It hath likewise been the common Opinion, that this must prove a new Bond of Affection between Relations, and engage them more heartily to promote each other's Good, whilst they considered, that they were of necessity to succeed each other in their Possessions. To this Point belongs the Passage of Plato, lib. xi. De Legibus, quoted by Grotius, and explained by Suetonius*.

His Panegyr. c. 37. highly commends, that the twentieth part was relieved to the Heirs of Families, Quod manifestum erat, quanto cum dolove latum, divin: aliquod, &c. because 'tis plain, that Men would bear it with great Grief, or rather never endure it, to have any defalked and taken from those Goods which they by Blood and Relation merited, and which they looked upon as their own, and to descend to the next akin, as their Inheritance.
And Publius Syrus faith, Havedem jire utilius est, quam quave re, i.e. It is better to know than seek an Heir, ver.255. And yet those Governments seem to have settled the Matter with most Prudence, which left Men the Privilege of disposing by Will those Goods only which they acquired by their proper Industry, ordaining, That whatever they received from their Patents or Anceftors, should pass down again to their nearest Relations. For by this Method all the Reasons produced on both sides of the present Question are most happily brought to a Temperament and Union.

It is altogether strange to the Manners and Customs of us Europeans, what we are told of the People of the Kingdom of Siam, That those who are Men of Substance among them, are commonly obliged to parcel out their Wealth into three Divisions, one of which goes to the King, another to the Priests (whence likewise the funeral Charges are defrayed) and the third only to the Children. And no less strange is the Practice of the Erhipiaus on the Coasts of Guinea ; where the Goods of either Parent do not descend to their Children, but to the nearest of their other Kindred.

On which Reason depends that disposition of the old Roman Law, which we meet with in 1. xxix. t. 2, 18. Dig. De acquir. vel omitt. heard.

Of Successions to Persons, &c.

Book IV.

XIX. The Heir by Will, and the Heir at Law, though they succeed in a different manner to their respective Estates, yet have this Obligation common to them both, viz. they shall discharge the Debts of the deceased, And that not so much on account of any tacit Engagement which they have entered into to this purpose*, as because these Debts are a necessary Burthen affecting the Possessions in the manner of a tacit Mortgage. For, as Quinétilian observes ', Such is the Nature and Condition of Inevitability, that the Creditors must first be satisfied before it can effectually take place. And so much only is to be reckoned a Man's Estate, as remains when all are paid their own ? Whence, likewise, is this most highly agreeable to natural Equity, that the Heir be not charged with Debts above the Value of the Inheritance. Nor should we omit what Gabriel the Stonite tells us in his Book of the Manners of the Eastern Nations, That the Mussulmans when they make their last Will, are bound to confess that they have taken by Robbery or Violence, to the proper Owner, from whom they receive a formal Discharge in Writing: And if they know not to whom Restitution should be made, they lay out a Sum in public Buildings, as Hospitals, Magazines, Bagnios, or cle bequeath it to the Poor, or some legal Order.

In Ferdinand Pinto, Cap. 21. the Chinese Herm advizeth Autony de Faria, who had been guilty of Sacrilege, to do these three things for his Soul's Health : to restore what he had taken away, to pardon for his Offences with Tears, and to distribute largely in Charity to the Poor. Add. Cap. 60.

Chapter XI.

Thirty Years Mankind seem to put on a new Face; it was thought very inconvenient that the following Age Should be disturbed upon every flight occasion.

Besides, when a Man had been without such a title to his Goods for thirty Years together, he was justly supposed to have settled quietly under the Loss; so that there was no need of troubling a Person on his account. The same reason will hold for that prescription which is sometimes allowed in criminal cases; it seeming unnecessary to bring to the Bar offences committed almost an age since, the ill effects of which time have sufficiently purged and effaced; so that the true end of punishment is superseded.

VI. But that prescription may effectually proceed, 'tis requisite that the Party, receiving the thing at the hands of a false Proprietor, do obtain this Potestas: by a just Title, or upon such grounds as are esteemed sufficient in other cases for the transferring and the acquiring of Property; and consequently to act in this matter bona fide and prescription.

Page 194. Edit. A Man cannot justly possess a thing merely by taxing it to his land, but by bidding it in secretly. Hence when the lands, which formerly belonged to King Apwi, were let to the Roman People, and every man took what part he liked best: Liniews calls this way of proceeding, Diutialecentia, A long continual Lice ness and Injustice.

According to the civil Laws 'tis enough it a Man had this due Piles, this rightnefs and Integrity of thought at his first entering on the Possession, though he happen afterwards to discover that the person who conveyed it to him was not the just Proprietor. But no Canon Law requires the same integrity through the whole term of years on which prescription is built; so that if a Man comes in the mean time to know that the thing was made over to him by one who had no right to dispute it, he begins immediately to be obliged to restore it to the lawful Owner, and from thenceforth detains it male side, tovily and dither cide, with that and honest intention; that is, that he be able to acknowledge a sufficient reason why he thus possesses it, and be persuaded in his mind, that the property was transferred really on him, and himdelf constructed true Owner. Liban, Declar. 5, especially in case he goes about to hide it from the Owner’s Knowledge by Craft and Delay, Which Judgment seems to approach nearest to the Strictness and Sanctity of the Law of Nature: Tnaimuch as, upon the introducing of distinct Proprietary rights, non excluditur, nunc viginti annus im ex Derivat. 5 Nir. Tawi maintains, That by natural Right an honest intention is not necessary to make a prescription even in the beginning of possession, provided so long a time is run out that it may reasonably be presumed that the true Proprietor has relinquished his possession of his goods. 'For, says he, in whatever manner we get into the possession of the goods that belong to another, 'from the moment that he to whom they belong, knowing that they are in our hands, and being able, if he pleases, to claim them, declares either expressly or tacitly, that he will let them rest there, we become the lawful owners of them as much as if we had a just title to them originally. Theodosius the younger, who established the prescription of thirty years, did not require any good intention in the possessor; 'twas Fustinian who introduced this maxim into the civil law. As for my self, Town, that if the true Master of a thing bought, or usurped and gotten from him, in a word, by foul dealing, does not put in his claim, nor declare any desire of recovering it for a long space of time, though he knows very well in whose hands it is, and there is nothing to hinder him from obtaining his right; in this case, I say, the unjust possessor becomes the lawful Proprietor, provided that he has somehow declared that he was ready to restore it if it had been demanded: for then the ancient owner acquits him, and manifestly renounces, though tacitly, all his pretensions to it. And thus our Author determines it in his Element. Furifprud. Univerf. p. 76,77. But if he that takes possession honestly of the goods of another comes to discover his error before the time of prescription is expired, he is obliged to do the duty of an honest possessor. See what is said in the next Chapter. But if, continuing always in his honest intention, he come to the time of prescription, whether it agree with the maxims of the natural law only, or the civil laws have reduced it to something less, the right of the ancient owner is entirely extinct, as I shall hereafter show. The whole amounts to this, that as the honest possessor who prescribes is the occasion, tho' innocent, that the other is debarred of all his pretensions, he ought to assist him as far as he can to revenge the wrong done by a third person who sold him the goods which he knew were not his own, and so was the cause of this prescription. In fine, though a good intention is always necessary to keep the conscience quiet, yet this is no impediment but that human laws may overlook this condition either wholly or in part, to avoid great numbers of actions. And to obtain this end, it may be very fit not to require a good intention in prescriptions, to which they have fixed so long a time, or to demand it at least in the beginning of possession; and so the maxim of the civil law in my judgment is better grounded than that of the canon law. The artifice of the clergy consists not so much in this, that the determinations of the popes require a perpetual good intention in him that prescribes, as in this, that they will have the goods of the church looked upon as not capable of being alienated, absolutely, or under such conditions as will make all prescriptions void. As for what Mr. Thomafius speaks of princes, who affirm that the demeans of the crown cannot be alienated justly, and that prescription has no place among such who have no dependence one upon another in a state of nature, see the last paragraph of this chapter, and Lib, viii. c. 5. §. 9. Chap. XII.

Third Party, the Person from whom we receive it
should be obliged to make it good; for after a course of Time thousands of Accidents might render him incapable of giving us this Satisfaction. And what grievous Commotions must shake the Commonwealth, if at so vast a distance of Years, so many Contracts were to be disannulled, so many Successions to be declared void, and so many Possessors to be ejected? It was therefore judged sufficient to allow such a Space, as large as in Reason could be desired, during which the lawful Proprietors might recover their own. But if through Sloth and Neglect they suffered it to slip; the Plaintiff might fairly reject their too late Importunity. And though it might so happen that now and then a particular Person lost his Advantage of recovering his Goods utterly against his Will, and without his Fault, only because he was unable to find out the Possessor; yet the Damage and Inconvenience arising from that general Statute to some few private Men, is compensated by the Benefit it affords to the Public. But we ought well to observe, That before we can charge the ancient Proprietor with Carelessness and Sloth, we must suppose, That he had a convenient Season to exert his Diligence.

Hence it is highly agreeable to Reason and Equity, that the time during which a Country hath been the Seat of War shall not avail towards Prescription: As Honorius particularly decreed, that no Space of Time in which the Vandals stood upon the Roman Ground should be reckoned towards the procuring of Prescription.

VI. But there is no Necessity, that, in order to assert the Justice of civil Governments, in establishing the Right of Prescription, we should have recourse (with a certain Author) to that Power of executing Punishment on the guilty, with which the chief Magistrate is invested. As if the Law denied an Action to those, who for so long a time forbore to challenge their own, for this reason only, because the Parties deserve to be put into the List of Criminals, for suffering Prescription to be pleaded against them; whilst by thus neglecting their Property, they not only prejudice the common Good of the Society, but likewise sin against their own Nature, which hath in all Cases an especial Regard to the public Advantage: And that therefore as soon ordained a Penalty against those who were idle and negligent, so here the Neglect of the Proprietor is punished with the Loss of his Property.

But indeed the principal Aim and Design of the Law concerning Prescription is not to punish Men's Defaults in this respect, but to provide, that the State be not disturbed by uncertain Titles, and by Properties in constant Doubt and Suspense. Though it is true, that by a Person's being denied to sue for Recovery, when he hath long neglected it, he suffers some Loss or Damage as a necessary Consequence.

Besides, to be excluded from some Advantage, lying open to those only who are vigilant and industrious in their own Affairs, doth not come up to the nature of a Punishment. For we certainly use a Figure when we say, that an idle Temper is a sufficient Revenge to itself: Or, That 'tis Punishment enough to the Lawful and unactive, that being put out from all Pits of Himur, they are constrained to pass their Days in Obscurity.

Besides, the Assertion is not true, That those who suffer their Goods to be withheld from them by Prescription, are really Offenders against the Commonwealth. They indeed do manifestly injure the Public, who either abuse and squander away their Substance, or whilst they sit brooding over it, and are Proprietors only in Name, let it grow useless for want of Application. But now a thing that is gained by Prescription, is however under the Care and Management of some Person; so as still to be serviceable to the Occasions of the Community. And 'tis altogether the same thing to the State whether such a Piece of Ground, for instance, be in the Hands of this Man or of that, provided it doth not lie quite neglected, without any one to cultivate and improve it.

To these Reasons we may add farther, That when any private Person receives Advantage from another's Punishment, 'tis necessarily supposed, that he was before considerably hurt or endamaged by the Party offending. Whereas he who commences a Proprietor by the Right of Prescription, can on no Account be said to have suffered Harm from the Neglect of the Party, whom he thus succeeds. Nor doth he rightly apply to the present Purpose those Words of Book xvi. t. 3. D. Depositi, Gen. Male mevitus publice, &c.

Since then the Law concerning Prescription is not a penal Statute, 'tis idle to dispute why the Negligence of the Proprietor should be rather punished by the Losses of the neglected Goods, than by some pecuniary Mulct. Though it is very evident that such a Mulct could not procure the true End of the civil Constitutions in this Affair, which was, To cut off all those Suits and Quarrels that would for ever have been springing up, and to entitle, at least, a quiet Enjoyment to long Possessors, whose Case entitles them to more than ordinary Favour.

For in the first place the Matter must have been brought into Court by the Claim of the former Proprietor, where the Cause would have been the more difficult and perplexed, by reason of the things continuing so long in other Hands; and then the present Possessor was to be ejected, whence a new Hardship would arise. For if the Fine were to go to the Magistrate, then the Possessor's just Title and honest Intentions were likely to stand him in no stead. Nor if the Possessor himself were to receive the Fine for a Comfort and Recompense, would all the Doubts be hereby resolved. Because, should the Fine be less in Value than what the Possessor loseth by quitting his Hold, he must still be, in part, a Sufferer: But were it as much, or more, then the ancient Claimant would get little by his Suit. Therefore there cannot be, in the Point before us, a more ready way to Peace and Quietness, than to declare, that after the Term of Years appointed for Prescription, the Right of the former Owner shall cease and be extinct.

VIL By what Law Prescription was first set on Foot, the learned are not well agreed: Most ascribe its Original to civil or positive Law, and oppose it to thefe Methods of Acquisition, which are commonly said to proceed from the Law of Nivias, Nas, Cajaminus, gous so far as to affirm, That Prescription doth really contradict the Law of Nations, in that it takes a Man's Property from him without his Consent: That it interferes likewise with natural Eynits, tho' only for the Sake of publick Good ; while it dannaigeth private Owners, but turns to the Benefit and Advantage of the Community. To which De Roy answers, 'That each particular Proprietor, by subjecting himself to thofe Laws which establish Prescription, doth at least implicitly consent to that Translation of his Right. Another Reason urg'd by Cujacius, to prove this Establishment to be contrary to the Law of Nations, is as follows: That, according to the faid Law, no Man can constitute ane as the true Proprietor of a thing, unless he were himself fo before : Whereas, by the civil Law, he who receives a thing from one who was not the Proprietor, may yet obtain the Property of it himfelf, if he can prescribe for it in the usual manner.

which De Roy* again replies, Thus in the Business of Prescription the Seller, or any other Non-proprietor, conveys more than the Title and honest Possession; but that the Property is wholly aided either by the standing Law, or by the publick Magiftrate, even according to the Law of Nations is invested with just Power to make new Ordinances, and to transfer Properties from one Person to another, cut out of a fair and reasonable Regard to the publick Good; the P, who thus suffers for his own Neglect, really consents to this Conveyance of his Property, or at least be prefumed to consent by his long Silence.

Some maintain Prescription to proceed from and positive Law, upon the Strength of this Argument; that in case a Man hath not originally obtained a Right on some other Bottom, the Length of Time can give none, as being defective of all Power to produce any Effect. For tho’ every Thing, fay they, is done in Time, yet Time itself doth nothing.

Now as to the Reason here propofed, thus must indeed be certain, That it depends wholly on the termination of positive Law, why Prescription should rather be completed at the Tenth or Twentieth Instance than at the Ninth, or the Sixteenth: Yet one can deny but that the Consent of all Nations to which they were moved by the Care of the common Peace, might be able to assign some rational Efficacy to the Course of Years; at least, far as that in Process of Time some certain Presumptions and Favours, on the side of Persons in Possession, should be granted to defend and confirm their Right, though attributed to other Cases than the bare Time itself. For tho’ pure natural Reafon, and the Agreement of all the W

do not fix any one Point of Time as the necessary Condition of obtaining a future Right, yet t

Lib. iii. tg. 8.

Foundation besides natural Right, yet 'tis not unjuft, that the Laws give it an Authority among Members of the same Kingdom.
For, as I shall show hereafter, 'tis so far from being contrary to natural Equity, that it is very conformable to it, and answers End and Deign of Prophecy. Upon the whole, a good Design is necessary to prescribe with a good Confcience, as to whether the civil Laws require it, or no. I also suppose, that Prescription is fixed at a time long enough, as we commonly reckon it. For, in my Judgment, an honest Man could less help himfelf among the Romans, when the Prescription of moveable Goods was made in one Year, and immoveable in two, in which the Emperor Fuffinian did acknowledge there was some Injuftice, as I have shown above, §. 5. n.4. Upon this ground Prescription is not an odious Right, nor conformable to natural Right, although Mr. Pacette fays 'tis, and in his Treatife of Reftitution, 1. v. c.6. compares it to an unjuft Arreft, yet does not free from the Obligation to Reftitution. He afferts, « That the Law of God does not admit of this Right, and the Jubile always restored the antient Proprietors to the Possession of their Goods, though voluntarily alienated.” But this has no relation to the Right of Prescription. God, for Reasons arising from the Constitution of the e:vish Republick, forbade the perpetual Alienation of their immoveable Eftates ; and not of their Goods in general, as Mr. La Placette expreffes it. See l.v. §. 4. following. In fine, there is nothing in the Law of Mojés that condemns Prescription as an unjuft Establishment, and can no more infer it from the Example he brings, than we may conclude that the perpetual Alienation of Lands is odious, and conformable to natural Right. The other Example which this Author adds, is not better apply'd. Although the Yebusites mistatn’d themselves feveral Years in the possession of the City of Ferulalem, after God had given the Children of Ijrael 6 Land of Caneax, yet Daviderove them from thence. This is a special Cafe, from which no Consequence can fairly be drawn, and Mr. La Placetie ought to remember, that when the Ammonites claimed certain Lands, which they affirmed to be theirs, oppofed them with this Argument, That the Jwelites had enjoy’d the peaceable Possession of them three hundred Years, which was enough to secure the Property to them. As to that other Reason offered by Grotius 3, to prove that a Devolution may be presumed from long Silence, because we must not believe that Men are so naturally itab; disposed towards each other as that they would suffer any Person to continue in a perpetual Conflict of Sin for the sake of a perishable Enjoyment, this does not at all affect the present Question. For, besides that it seems a little too simple to flatter ourselves with so large Promises of Men's Consciences and Piety; he that comes to a Possession by honest Means, and with Innocency of Intention (and him only we have pronounced capable of commencing Proprietor by Prescription) is really in no Sin; because the manner of his obtaining the Possession fully persuades him, that he obtained the Property together with it. And it does not appear that any Man is obliged voluntarily to call in question his own Right, established upon a lawful and probable Title. But if the detaining of another’s Goods after this manner were indeed in itself sinful, the Guilt were to be taken off, not by the Silence of the Owner, but by his exprefs Concession.

In teeth the Silence of the Proprietor proceeds commonly from thele things only, viz. either he knows not who has his Goods, or he is ignorant of his own Right to them, or he hath some Reason, more or lefs strong, why he does not put in his Claim. Of the Obligations which arise

Book IV.

CHAP. XI
Of the Obligations which arise immediately from Property,

1. Every one is obliged to abstain from another's
Goods.

31. Others' Goods kept by us are to be restored,

iv. Which is proved,

iv. And illustrated.

v. Contracts made about others' Goods are void, as
soon as they are known.

vi. What is gained by another's Goods must be restored.

vii. An honest Possessor is not bound to restore, if the
Goods have decayed, or lost.

viii. But he is bound to restore the present Fruits.

ix. And such as are spent, if he must have spent
others of the like Value.

His enquired into the Nature and Origin
of Property, as likewise into the several ways
by which it is established, it follows that we consider those Obligations, which, upon the introduction of Property, affect Mankind immediately * and
on their own Account, without the Intervention
of other Duties. Of these the first is, That every
Man shall suffer another, who is not engaged in
Hostility against him, to dispose of his own Possessions, and likewise quietly to hold and enjoy
them ; nor shall, either by Force or Fraud, impair,
divert, or draw them to himself. Whence it appears, that Theft*, Rapine, removing of Boundaries, and the like Crimes are forbidden by the
bare Law of Nature. Euripides * speaks excellently
to this purpose ;

God hates the violent, commanding all}

To live on what their honest Pains procure ;

And not to feed their Wants with mutual Spoils,
Opprobers should be banished human Race,
Unworthy of the Name. One common Heaven
Gives Light and Air to Man; one Earth a Seat,
A Scene of Industry, where all may strive

To raise their Stock, and spread their Fortunes wide ;
But not to rob, or force their Neighbour’s fore.

* Vid. D. Lib. x. t. 4. 11. 33. De fugitic.

x. But not them he has neglected to gather.

II. Further, When the things of one Man come
into the hands of another without the latter’s
free consent (where under the general Name of
things we comprehend likewise our Right over
Persons, so far as it may be profitable to us, as
the Right of Masters over their Servants), we are
to consider, whether the thing be still remaining,
or not.

As to things which remain, there arises the
Obligation concerning them ; That he, who is in
possession of what belongs to us, ought to employ
his utmost Ability towards putting it again under
our Command. Which Obligation does not exist
force, till such time as the Party in Possession
comes to know that the thing is ours.

We add, That he employs his utmost Ability,
or does as much as in him lies ; for no one can be
bound to an impossible Performance. Nor is he
obliged to put himself to Charges in making the
restitution and whatever Expences he has been at
on that Account, he may fairly demand of the
Owner, and may detain the thing till they are
paid. But 'tis enough if he signify, that another's
Goods are in his Hands *, and that he will be no
hindrance to the Owner in the Recovery of them.

Cuap. XIII.

By others' fiat, if a finder takes up another's thing with a design to convert it to his own use, he is guilty of theft, whether he knows the particular owner or not. Yet, if I become master of a thing upon a just title and with hostile intention, I am not bound to call my own right into dispute and give public notice that such a thing is in my custody, to the end that it may be challenged if it should happen to belong to another. For when the manner of my getting possession was in no respect faulty, my innocence and integrity clear me from all imputation of guilt in detaining another's goods.

This further restriction is likewise to be understood in the present duty: If he who was before the true owner has still any probable means left of his recovering what he lost; that the obligation we are now alerting may not be thought to overthrow the right of prescription.

III. Now that this obligation is sufficiently founded in the bare notion of property, appears evident. For since a person may happen, by many accidents, to lose his hold and be thrown out of possession of what is really his own; our goods, and especially those which are movable, would be in a very slippery and uncertain condition. For if, when they stray into another's hands, he might intercept or conceal them from us, more so if he might detain such a thing openly and repulse us with violence when we attempted to make good our claim. And therefore, as in a rate of communion it is a matter of chance that each person shall be allowed to use the common store as fully and freely as the rest; so upon the first appropriation of things, when all other persons did, as it were, renounce their right to what any one had received by private seizure, the distinct proprietors are supposed to have made this agreement among themselves: that he who takes possession of another's goods, after believing them his own, should cause them to revert to him, over and above, for the power and virtue of property would be too weak, and the keeping of things would require too much expense, as well as too much care and trouble, if these stray'd goods were only to be restored when the owner made a formal challenge of them; because he must very frequently be ignorant which way they are gone or where they are lodged.

As to a man's being bound to restore a thing when claimed by the owner, it is altogether the same case whether he got possession by honest or dishonest means: For this obligation does not arise from any default or any fact of curs. Mr. Bare notes on §. 1, 11.

T The edition of the work put out in 1706 adds, after Vitin, these words: Aut si, if we have the least suspicion that the thing left to us, we must not take it and if we do receive it, we reduce ourselves to a necessity of restoring it if it proves true.

1 There is no need of supposing such a general agreement as we have proved upon c 4, 6. Goods of another is as natural a consequence of property as it is not to take them.

But this obligation ought to be understood in such a manner as not to destroy the rights of an honest possession or a putative property, which, as I have before observed, §.. Note 3., produces the same effect as a property more real and incontrovertible, so long as the real owner appears not. This neither Grotius, nor our author, nor any other that I know of, were aware of, and therefore have been puzzled very much to determine several cases which have fallen in upon this subject, and so many times their solutions were inconsistent one with another, which proves sufficiently that their principle upon which they argued was not found. I say then, that one of the principal uses of our goods being to trade withal, and that use requiring that the honest possessor should be reputed in all respects the lawful proprietor, such a possessor can be obliged to restore only what is in being, i.e., what he has not parted with, nor is in any manner perished; for he then has nothing, and so can restore nothing, as our author himself acknowledges, respecting what is given away or sold again as it was acquired, and to what is spent or lost. Moreover, all that the honest possessor hath done, or performed, as such, upon the account of the goods of another, which he believed his own, is as valid as to him as if he had disposed of a thing to him, of whom no other person can claim anything, and the profit, which might redound to him by such goods, while he was in possession of them, or when he parted with them, belongs to him by consequence. For as he was, and ought to be supposed the true proprietor, the rights and profits of the property did absolutely accrue to him, so he had no reason to suppose otherwise. And then if the ancient owner recovers his goods, he begins, as we may say, expense, to lose them. The peaceful enjoyment of the honest possessor is, a hindrance to the power of the true proprietor, but insures to the putative proprietor the fruits of his management, while he retains authority. This being agreed on, we may see in my judgment how far the natural obligation of restoring the goods of another extends when men have had an honest possession with a just title. If he hath disposed of them by any good and irrevocable act to a third person, who has honestly received them, he is only obliged to assist, as much as he can, the old owner to make and retain his goods, to give him satisfaction. For the true proprietor, that he may do what he ought in the case. But if the thing is yet in the hands of the honest possessor, has got the possession of it without charge, or it has cost him something. In the first case, as when a person has offered to take a thing, he ought to return it with the same care and diligence with which he received it. In the other case, if one has bought it, or taken it to himself, the true owner, who would recover his goods, should repay the honest possessor what he has given, otherwise, he may keep the thing; and if the other do not redeem it before the time of prescription is come, it then changes the owner, so that the first can have no title to it. By these principles it is easy to determine clearly all the questions which can arise on this matter, as we shall see in the notes upon the following paragraphs, where I shall reflect our author not of the same sentiments with Grotius, yet he reasons in general according to the notions of the civil laws of several people, and seems to overrule him here. This I mention not by mere conjectures for in his elements of law, the first work that I attempted to comment on, he took notice of the weakness of Grotius's opinion, manner, as can't be well grounded but by supposing the principles that I have distinctly established.

From any particular Covenant made with the Claimant, but from the thing itself; or rather from that general Covenant to this purpose, which we suppose to be the necessary attendant of Property. He who obtained the thing honestly is merely obliged to make restitution; but he who procured it dishonestly, besides the necessity of restitution, has also contracted a guilt and is on that account liable to punishment. Good Faith, or honest intention, does then cease, at least in the Court of Conscience, when a Man has full assurance that what he holds belongs to another. Though it is enough to secure him from human punishment if he were thus well-meaning and sincere at his first entering on possession.

IV. This is confirmed and illustrated by the Divine Law itself, Deut. xxii. 1, 2, 3. And lest any should imagine that the duty there enjoined is to be paid to friendship only, 'tis expressly added, Exod. xxiii. 4, that the same ought to be performed to an Enemy.

Josephus has given us this gloss on the Law with which we are now mentioning: If any Man, says he, finds Gold or Silver in his way, let him seek out the Party who left it, and restore it by the hands of the public Crier, in the very place where he took it up, judging with himself that no advantage would be good which arises from another's damage. The same must do with regard to the stray Sheep and Cattle he meets with in the Desert. If he cannot presently find out the Owner, let him retain the things in his own custom, calling God to witness that he intended not to make a gain of what belonged to his Neighbour. Yet the mortal hatred which the Jewish Nation professed against all others, afterwards turned this natural into a civil Law, to be put in practice only towards their own Countrymen.

One of the most remarkable instances of restitution which History affords is that of the Emperor Trajan, who, when a Woman cried after him in his progress and claimed the Horse on which he rode, finding upon enquiry that the Governor of a certain Province had taken it away and presented it to him in his own name, he immediately gave back the Horse to the poor Woman; and having no others at hand from his own stable, was content to make use of the next he could borrow. Which, they tell us, was the rise of that custom which afterwards obtained for the Emperors to carry in their train a great number of horses, for supplies, in case of any such accident.

The example of the Spartans, which Grotius mentions, who condemned their General Phabidas for seizing on the Cadmean Fort and yet still kept the place in their hands, does not come up to our point: For they were, no doubt, injurious and dishonest possessors, and therefore were bound to restitution by another principle. Nor is the story of MM. Crassus and Q. Curtius more proper in the present question, as Tully gives report: Some persons brought out of Greece to Rome a forged will of L. Minucius Bililius, a very wealthy man, and the more easily carry their point, put down M. Crassus and Q. Curtius, two of the greatest power and later in the city, as joint heirs with them. The two Gentlemen, though they suspected the deed to be counterfeit, yet relying upon their own innocence in the matter, did not refuse to make this small advantage of the others' wickedness. What then? Is it enough that they appear to save no advantage in the fact? I am not of that opinion: For he certainly is to be condemned as unjust who not only forbears to drive off injury from another but aids and encourages it. The Gentlemen had as great a share in the crime of forgery as receivers are said to have in that of theft, inasmuch as they pretended themselves to have been put into the will for no other reason but that their name and authority might protect the authors of the cheat.

From the same head we may discover the custom of awarding wrecks to the Prince or to the State to be disagreeable to equity. As we may

O> "There are some priests in Germany, where the Preachers refuse not to pray to God in the pulpit that he would make more shipwrecks upon their coasts. And Mr. Thom maintains that neither these prayers nor the custom itself are absolutely unreasonable or disagreeable to the rules of charity or justice; for though, as he says, in the time of the wreck there is no design to abandon utterly what is cast away, yet there is no hope ordinarily of recovering it, and we know that there is as much reason to fear that the goods are utterly lost as if they had been cast into the main ocean: besides, the owner of the coasts may, at the place where he has a right to demand customs of strangers, use all means to repay himself for the expenses he is at in maintaining the port and shore. We may add to this, that it is often very hard to know whose goods and merchandise those are that the sea throws upon the shore. So that they are a kind of alluvions, which, by the right of nations, is a lawful way of getting. The public prayers made on this subject ought not to be understood as if they besought of God that he would make a greater number of shipwrecks, but only that he would caution that the sea should not retain the goods cast into it, but discharge them well of them by casting them upon their coasts rather than any other; for what reason is there for us to suppose that such holy churchmen should every day beg God's help for a thing contrary to all natural right? Or, at least, that some of their brethren should not charitably advise them of such a detestable sin, which they had been guilty of so long a time? Thefe are the reasons of the author of whom he speaks, which he delivers in his discourse, De Statuum Imperii potestate Legiflatoria Fas commuynes printed at Hall in 1793, §. 42. The manner in which he justifies the prayers to manifestly appears absurd (to speak no worse of them) would make us believe that he is not in earnest, and that he diverts himself with want of conscience in the clergy. As for the confiscation of the goods belonging to such as have suffered shipwreck, the proprietors who cast them away do not look upon them altogether lost, but that they reserve to themselves a right of claiming them if ever they happen to be cast upon the shore, as they know it often comes to pass. See above, c.6. §.122. And 'tis not by these misfortunes that the maintenance of ports and shore ought to be upheld: The toll would be too exorbitant and odious; such as lose their goods would at this rate pay for those that have the good luck to save them, and get to the end of their voyage. That it is no less shipwreck than if it happened in the main sea shows plain enough how frivolous the practice is.

Cuar. XI.

May likewise gather the Absurdity of that Practice in some Countries, by which the stolen Goods, when discovered, are not restored to the Owner, but are claimed by the public Treasury.

V. Inasmuch as this Engagement to restore the Goods of others ariseth from a general Agreement among all Mankind, a Bar is hereby put to all particular Contracts made about a thing which is any way kept from the true Owner; the Effect of which is, that when the thing is known to be another’s, any Bargain about the conveying it to a third Party becomes null and void. And this root is the ground of Diogenes's Jest on two Thieves, one of which had stolen something, but the other had lost nothing.

As to that Law of the Digest, produced by Zieoler, to prove that a Contract made after such a Discovery is not always evacuated or hindered by the Force of Property, it is really no prejudice to what we now assert: For in the Case there alleged, the Interest of the Creditor is more concerned that the Pledge should remain safe, than the Interest of the Debtor who owns it; and the Debtor cannot challenge the Pledge, unless upon Payment.

The Judgment of Tryphouinus, in the same place of the Digest, upon the other Case which he there propoundeth, doth not to me appear satisfactory. A Man cast for a Capital Crime, saith he, hath deposited an hundred Pounds in your Hands; the Man afterwards transported, and his Goods confiscated; the Question is, Whether you shall vestore the hundred Pounds to him who gave it you in Chancery, or else to pay it into the Treasury. If we consider the Law of Nautius and Nustinus 3, the Money is to be given back to the Party who committed it to your care; but if we consider the End of civil Government, and the Rule and Manner of Laws, your case rather is to throw it into the public Treasury, for he who hath deserved it of the whole State should not struggle with Poverty among his other Tribulations, that his Example may deter others from such Enne. 

But, indeed, since for foreign Rulers have even by the Law of Nations a Power to punish Criminals in their Fortunes and Estates; when such a Penalty is justly agreed against a Malefactor, 'tis agreeable to the very Law of Nature that all his Goods should be forfeited to the Government: Yet that the Confiscation of Goods should attend any one particular Crime rather than others, is purely owing to the Appointment of positive Constitutions. The consideration of that Benefit which accrues to the Public from Penalties duly inflicted (the Reason urged by Tryphouinus) did indeed show that such a penal Sanction ought to be approved of; but it was not properly the Rule, why the Treasury should have the advantage of the Criminal, as to challenging the Sum which he had lodged in other Hands. For by the Sentence of the Curia all the Right and Property of the condemned Criminal over his Goods was taken from him, and converted on the Government; and consequently what he formerly gave in Trust is to be delivered back, not to him, but to the publick.

Receivers. Because all kinds of property, whether from positive ordinances or from the law of nations, has this among others: that he who is in possession of any thing over which the said property extends, shall be bound to restore it to the party who at present appears to be the true owner. What demurs and exceptions the law of repossessing things given in charge admits in other cases upon account of particular circumstances, is frequently shown by authors. Vid. Cre. Oud. iii. c. 25; Sewecu De Benct. i. iv. c. 10; Ambr. De Of. L. c. ult. To which may be added what Polybius (in excerpt. Peirefc. p. 172.) reports of Aviavathes, King of Cappadie, who having recovered the kingdom from Orophernes, demanded of the Pythians the forty talents which Orophernes had put into their hands; and upon their refusing to deliver them to him, fell upon their city with fire and sword, in Polybius’s opinion very unjustly. Upon this action of Aviavathes may be commended, it we first suppose that Orophernes had injuriously deprived him of his crown.

Upon this natural obligation to restitution, the compilers of the civil law have built a great number of additional rules. And this too is the ground of claiming by judicial process what is detained from us, together with all the actions which border on that claim; and in some sort, the action of false debt; the action for recovery of what we have given, either upon some reason which reason has not been made good, or else upon no reason at all. Though these actions are said likewise to depend upon a kind of imaginary contract. For when we deliver a thing without intending it for a matter of pure bounty, it is supposed to be given by the one party and received by the other on this condition: that it shall be delivered back, in case there appear no reason why it was given.

What has been said about the restitution of the main thing or substance extends likewise to the fruits or profits of it, such as are now remaining; Mr. Barz. NOTES on §, v, vi.

VI. But if what we have honestly gotten, though really belonging to another, has been honestly spent, then it seems most agreeable to natural equity that we should not pay the whole value of it to the owner, but only the advantage they brought us, or so much as we were made the richer by it; provided still that the owner has not been requited for what he lost, some other way. For if honestly acquire and consume what was taken from you, when you have already received full satisfaction from the thief, you can then demand nothing of me, how much soever I have been the gainer by my bargain. The ground and reason of this assertion is not so much to be sought from the end of property (which was established that every man might, according to proportion, enjoy his own: whereas he who gains by it is mine, hath more than his proportion, as I on the contrary have less) as from the following consideration; that a thing in which I have not my property, either by my own free consent, by default, or by the right of war, still belongs to me; as doth likewise all the fruit and product of it. When such a thing therefore has fallen into another man’s hands, who has made an advantage by spending it; his honesty and good intention secure him indeed from all guilt and sure; yet he can on no pretence withhold the profits, when I lay claim to them, because they are to be looked on as the residue, or the surviving part of the thing, at least they are the proper and necessary fruit proceeding from it. Hence is one of the most common and proverbial sayings, that a man ought to gain by another’s loss, that is, by such a loss as he did not himself procure, either by his consent or default, so as to be the cause of the damage, or to have it any way imputed to him. For it can be no sin in me to take an occasion of advantage from another’s loss or damage when it was not my own.

11 In the opinion of the Roman lawyers there is no obligation to another which is not founded on the consent of him who is bound by it. When there appears no signs of a consent in certain things, wherein men are nevertheless obliged, they suppose it, and call it a quass contract. But in all the cases that they allege on this occasion, and which respect the management of another’s business by commitment; the transacting of public affairs in societies; the administration of a guardianship; the admission or acceptance of an inheritance, and the payment of a thing not due. In all these cases the obligation proceeds either from a tacit agreement, properly so called, or from a positive law, or from some maxims of moral equity only, and there is no need of feigning the formal consent of a person wholly ignorant of what passes. But it is to be considered likewise,
whether the present be still remaining in the last
receiver’s hands or not: If it be, the proprietor
shall claim it directly of him, and not trouble
the intermediate receiver: If not, the main burden
shall still fall on the person who either now
possesses the thing, or hath been made richer by
it. The intermediate possessor shall only come in
for a small share in the burden, inasmuch as he
perhaps had an opportunity of making some
advantage.

VI. Sixthly, if such a possessor, having

he shall still be bound to give the owner any more
than one plus of the price cost? or so much as he

nothing and yet he hath sold it, he shall then be
obliged to give up the price received; in which
case the owner cannot have the thing itself of the

have squandered away the price taken, which,
if not so easily gotten, had not been so properly
spent. But he who puts a thing off just so much
as it cost him, is no gainer, being supposed only
to recover his own. Nor can it be said in this
case that the price supplies the room of the thing
unless he parted with it out of knavish design:
because otherwise the owner may challenge his
goods from the hands of him who is now in
possession.

There is a law of the Digest urged in the
present case, which runs thus; if after a thief
hath sold the goods he stole, the owner of the
same by diligent means get the price out of his
adversary, he seems to be guilty of robbery as
much as the other party was before, and to be
equally obnoxious to the law. For all agree,
that the advantage of a stolen thing, or the money
into which it is turned, is not itself likewise stolen.
But this law properly respects civil governments,
for those who live under them are presumed to
have some right to their possessions.

Chap. XIII.

In a State of natural Liberty, may as fairly seize by violence the price of what hath been stolen from them, as the thing itself.

NIL. Seventy, such a purchase, though be purchased the thing at a considerable expense, yet is bound to deliver it, and cannot require his charges of the owner, but by the sheriff. For, otherwise, the right of challenging what is thine to no account, if the challenger were to refund the price. And he who buys a thing of another, whom he might suspect not to be the true proprietor, might to have provided particularly for his own security, in case the thing should afterwards happen to be his. Though this condition of securing the buyer's title is indeed implied in all contracts of sale, according to natural equity.

To the rule above-mentioned the following exception ought to be added: If in a case where the true proprietor could not in all probability have recovered possession of his own without some expense: as suppose the goods were detained in the hands of thieves and sometimes purchased. For here the honest man, who delivers the goods, may fairly deduct so much as the proprietor would have gladly spent to regain them: because the actual possession, especially when not to be recovered without difficulty, is capable of being rated at a certain value, and the proprietor, when re-instituted in it, is accordingly so much the richer. Whence arose the custom for persons who have lost anything to promise a reward and encouragement to the finder. For the same reason, though the buying of what's already our own be void, according to the ordinary course of the civil law, yet Paulus affirms it to be good and valid if it were agreed upon that the possession of what's our own may be purchased, when remaining with another.

'Tis proposed as a farther question on this point, whether a man who buys a thing thus detained, purely with design to convey it to the owner, may demand the price to be refunded? Some take the negative part; because, say they, the right accruing to the proprietor cannot be taken off by this allegation of the buyer. But indeed, if such a purchaser foresaw with fair probability that the true owner would immediately from property, and if the price which he gave does not exceed what the actual possession would he rated at, then it is absolutely requisite that what he expended should be repaid him. But whether he who redeems the thing in this case shall be allowed an action against the proprietor, as they term negotiorum gestorum, or to recover the charges he has been at in the proprietor's business, it is the province of the civilians more nicely to weigh and enquires " PHEREAHOL, since Greene thinks it ought to be omitted, because the afore-said action ariseth purely from the civil law, having mine of these futurities to vel vpe, from which bare nature introduces an obligation in the case. But though 'tis not indeed the concern of the law of nature to examine or determine to what particular actions civil law the present case may be, or could be reduced; yet it cannot be denied but that the very action above specified, of recovering charges on account of business managed for another, hath a foundation in natural equity, and in tacit consent. For it cannot on any pretence be required of me, that I should by my kind and generous assistance preserve or improve another man's goods altogether gratuitously, and without receiving what I am out of pocket in his service. It seems therefore the most plain and natural way of resolving such cases, that the party who redeems a thing after this manner, as likewise he who transacts any business on another's behalf, be supposed to hold the thing which he hath redeemed, or about which he hath employed his money or his pains, as a pledge or mortgage, till such time as he receives satisfaction. Yet if there be no fruits of his labour remaining, which he might take hold on for his own security, and if the other barbarously deny to pay him for his useful and profitable assistance, I am not of opinion that he may apply the same means towards allorting his right as are used in that other kind of right which arises from express contract; but all he can do shall be to expose the ungrateful wretch to public hatred and detestation, as one who does not deserve the least instance of good will.

BOOK V.

Of PRICE.

2. What is the moral quantity of things. The common price is not sufficient for the commerce of man’s life.

3. How many kinds of price.

4. What is the foundation of the common price of things.

8. Why the prices of things rise.

9. Of the price of fancy.

Mr. Barz. NOTES ON CHAP. I. §. 1.

* Commerce is a consequence of the property of goods, and price is the consequence of commerce, or a thing necessary to accommodate each other by way of exchange, to which all commerce in general is to be reduced. So that the rule of law
for the settlement of commerce should be referred to the law of nations, understood in the manner I have explained elsewhere, in cap. 3. §. 23.

1. Tit. 1. De Jus & Jure, leg. 5. Mr. Thomafius nevertheless maintains that commerce is not the law of nations farther,
than by assuming that right from such general customs as have proceeded from the corrupted manners of mankind, and which are
settled by corrupted reason; seeing that the necessity, diversity, and great increase of commerce is the effect of vice, and the
growth of it. See the discourse, De Faure Statu et Conditi Cwitatis, §. 14., and that, De Pre SO
Bes Hox ca. Chap. i. §. 5. both printed at Hoifin Suny. But this rather relates to divinity, than the civil law. (See id. i. cap. 1. §. 11. above.) It is sufficient, that in the state that things now are, commerce,
as well as property of goods, is necessary among men in the condition they are, so that we may say, that the settlement of commerce in general is very conformable to the most pure reason, and the law of nations, so called in the most agreeable sense. Lastly,
commerce is a consequence, and one of the chief uses of property, we must be careful not to extend the right of property beyond its due limits.

TL We find then, that Things are said to be equal, but only as they agree in some Dimensions, but in other respects not. Thus Honour, Labour, and Wages are said to be equal or unequal, not by reason of their agreeing or disagreeing in Dimension, but upon some other account. And therefore there must be some other Quantity, besides that which is termed Physical and Mathematical, though Philosophers have hitherto talked of no other. Which is evident, if we consider, that the Nature of Quantity in general does not consist in the Extension of Substance, but in Things being capable of having a Value put upon them, and consequently of being compared together. But since things receive a Value, not only from their natural Substance, but also in respect of some moral Consideration; it follows, that besides the natural there must be also a moral Quantity *. However, Things of the same Nature and Goodness receive a Value even from their natural Quantity, as a great Diamond is more valuable than a small one; which yet we have not always a regard to in the Valuation of Things of a different Species or Goodness; for a great Dog is not always more valuable than a little one, or a great Mass of Lead than a small piece of Gold.

How Persons are morally valued according to Opinion, and their Actions, according as they are productive of Merit or Demerit, has already been discussed in its proper place *. My design here is only to treat of the moral quantity of Things and Agens, as they are conceived to have some use in the common Affairs of Life, and as they are capable of being compared together in order to Commerce. This we call Price, which is the moral Quantity Value, or what is equal to it, to be compared with another in order to Trade.

III. Price may be divided into * proper and eminently; the first is placed in Things and Actions, so far as they are capable of procuring either the Necessaries, or Conveniences, or Pleasures of Life: the other is placed in Money, which is supposed to contain virtually the Prices of all Things else, and to be the common Measure and Standard of them.

IV. For the right understanding the Nature of the proper Price, it is necessary to consider distinctly,
